12. 2026 elections

12.1 Electoral reform

12.1.1 The BTI 2026 report noted:

‘Upon assuming power, the IG formed the so-called Election Reform Commission to ensure transparency and greater electoral fairness. It ultimately made more than 150 recommendations across 16 key areas. For example, legislation should be enacted to establish a permanent national constitutional council responsible for appointing members to constitutional bodies such as the Election Commission. The Election Commission should also be empowered to suspend or cancel elections in cases of malpractice, appoint its secretaries independently and, with unanimous approval, delay elections for up to 90 days during anticipated crises. Another recommendation was for the Election Commission to declare the credibility of elections within 48 hours of the results, enabling aggrieved parties to file appeals with the Constitutional Council or the Appellate Division. Lastly, a specialized cadre for Election Commission officials should be established to ensure professionalism and independence in election management.’[footnote 99]

12.1.2 Regarding co-operation between political parties and the interim government, the same report stated:

‘… In recent months … political parties, the interim government (IG) and reform commissions have begun working together to implement reforms to strengthen internal democracy, increase transparency in candidate selection and limit the influence of dynastic leadership. These efforts also include proposals to enforce mandatory internal elections, introduce campaign finance regulations and establish codes of conduct for party operations to ensure greater accountability and reduce factionalism.’[footnote 100]

12.1.3 In February 2026, International IDEA interviewed Md Abdul Alim, a member of the Electoral Reform Commission. The article noted that:

‘… the interim government has taken important steps to bolster the credibility of the upcoming election. He [Alim] states that “roughly 50 of the Electoral Reform Commission’s 250 recommendations have already been adopted into Bangladesh’s legal framework. These include strengthening the Election Commission’s administrative powers, provisions for overseas voting and measures to increase polling transparency.” Moreover, the law now bans party figures from remaining inside polling stations throughout the voting process (previously a common practice …), giving the presiding officer authority to remove and take legal actions against them.

‘While these changes improve past electoral management practices, Alim notes that many electoral reforms remain pending, such as the independent appointment of election commissioners, among broader proposals in the July Charter.’[footnote 101]

12.1.4 For information on other reforms proposed by the IG, see Legislative, constitutional and policy reform.

12.2 Political participation

12.2.1 On 25 December 2025, BBC News reported:

‘Tarique Rahman, the front-runner to be the next prime minister of Bangladesh, has returned to the country after 17 years in exile ahead of landmark general elections… Rahman’s return comes in the wake of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina being ousted last year.

‘He had been the subject of various criminal investigations launched while her Awami League party was in power but was cleared of all charges when her regime fell.’[footnote 102]

12.2.2 The EU EOM April 2026 report stated: ‘On 11 December 2025, the Bangladesh Election Commission (EC) announced that parliamentary elections would be held on 12 February 2026, concurrently with a referendum on the July National Charter.’[footnote 103]

12.2.3 In relation to voter registration, the EU EOM 2026 report noted:

‘… more than 127.7 million voters registered for these elections, an increase of 8 million compared with the January 2024 poll …

‘Under the active registration system, eligible citizens must apply to be included on the lists …The voter lists closed on 31 October 2025, with voters who turned 18 before that date being eligible for inclusion. The completeness and accuracy of voter lists was assessed positively by most EU EOM interlocutors …’[footnote 104]

12.2.4 Regarding political party campaigning, the same report noted:

‘The campaign was pluralistic, dynamic and competitive, and voters were presented with a wide choice of distinct political agendas. Fundamental freedoms of assembly and expression were generally respected. While political parties were overall able to compete on a level playing field, in some constituencies some candidates benefited from close links with district or local authorities, as well as unequal access to financial resources. Of the 50 contesting parties, only four conducted nationwide campaigns, with the BNP and JeI being most visible, and the IAB [Islami Andolan Bangladesh] and NCP present to a lesser extent. Candidates relied on a wide range of campaign methods, including outdoor advertising, in-person events, street campaigning, and digital outreach. Senior party figures, such as BNP’s Tarique Rahman and JeI’s Shafiqur Rahman, led high-profile rallies attended by tens of thousands and followed live on Facebook by over 40 million viewers each. The EU EOM observed 190 in-person campaign events, most of which were peaceful, and had adequate police protection, although confrontational rhetoric emerged at times. In the digital space, official party and candidate pages were primarily used for self promotion, while unofficial supporting accounts were often used for attacking opponents. The tone of the campaign hardened closer to elections, with parties frequently accusing each other of creating an uneven playing field, and of threats and violence.’[footnote 105]

Political demonstrations and rallies continue to take place in Bangladesh. However, there are periodic reports of tensions and clashes between supporters of different political groups.

What is the police response to protest? Are there differences in response under the Awami League, the Interim Government and the current government?

The July-August 2024 protests were marked by significant unrest and the use of force by security forces, which subsequently became the subject of domestic and international scrutiny and prompted wide-ranging discussions on police reform and accountability.

Following the July 2024 Uprising and political transition, police reform was identified as a priority area by the interim government and examined through the Police Reform Commission. The EU Election Observation Mission found that the 2026 elections took place in a substantially different environment, describing the elections as credible and noting that polling day was peaceful. Nonetheless, it recorded sporadic localised political violence and highlighted concerns regarding protection from harassment and intimidation in some instances.

What were the levels of pre-election / election period intra- and inter-party violence? How does this compare to levels under the Awami League?

The EU Election Observation Mission (EU EOM) assessed the 2026 parliamentary elections as credible and genuinely competitive, noting that fundamental freedoms were broadly respected and that polling day was peaceful. The EU EOM nevertheless recorded sporadic localised incidents of political violence and intimidation during the campaign period.

Observers generally noted a more open and competitive political environment than during recent electoral cycles. The EU EOM described the polls as the first genuinely competitive parliamentary elections since 2008 and highlighted a revitalised civic space during the campaign period.

Any inter- / intra-party violence post-election? What was the police response?

There have continued to be reports of localised incidents of both inter-party and intra-party violence following the election, particularly in relation to local political rivalries, competition for influence and disputes within party structures. However, these incidents have generally been localised rather than indicative of widespread national unrest.

The police have continued to respond through their normal law enforcement responsibilities, including maintaining public order, providing security at political events, investigating allegations of violence and making arrests where offences are alleged to have occurred. However, a number of observers have noted continuing challenges in relation to law and order and public confidence in law enforcement following the events of 2024.

Any violence by the state? If so, by whom and, if security forces, which security forces?

Since the political transition of August 2024, allegations of violence or misconduct by state actors have continued to be reported, although the scale and nature of such allegations differ from those associated with the July-August 2024 protests. Reporting by human rights organisations and other observers has focused primarily on allegations relating to arrests, detention practices, treatment of individuals in custody, and the conduct of security forces in maintaining public order.

Where allegations have involved security forces, they have most commonly concerned the Bangladesh Police, including metropolitan and district police units responsible for law enforcement and public order functions. Human rights organisations have also continued to monitor the conduct of other security and intelligence agencies.

Questions relating to accountability, oversight of security institutions, police reform and public confidence in law enforcement remain part of the broader governance and reform agenda that emerged following the political transition.

Can journalists operate freely? Are there legal or practical barriers?

Journalists in Bangladesh continue to report on a wide range of political, social and economic issues. The 2026 EU Election Observation Mission noted a revitalised civic space and found that fundamental freedoms were broadly respected during the election period.

At the same time, journalists continue to face legal and practical challenges, including concerns relating to digital security legislation, online harassment, disinformation, self-censorship and pressures associated with reporting on politically sensitive issues. The EU EOM also highlighted incidents of digital violence and harassment and noted concerns regarding the adequacy of protection for media actors in some cases.

Domestic and international organisations have also raised concerns regarding criminal proceedings involving some journalists and the potential impact of such cases on media freedom and freedom of expression.

Women journalists may face additional challenges, including gender-based harassment and abuse, particularly in online spaces.

Can NGOs / CSOs operate freely? Are there legal or practical barriers?

Civil society organisations, NGOs, think tanks, professional associations and advocacy groups continue to operate in Bangladesh and play an active role in public life, development activities and policy discussions. Since the political transition of August 2024, civil society actors have participated in consultations on governance and institutional reform, and many observers have noted a more open civic environment than in previous years.

At the same time, NGOs and CSOs continue to operate within a regulatory framework that includes requirements relating to registration, funding, reporting and compliance. Organisations working on governance, human rights and politically sensitive issues may encounter administrative, legal or operational challenges.
